speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: To encourage families to support one another in their retirement years, CPF members who have met their own retirement needs can transfer their CPF savings to their spouses, parents, grandparents, parents-in-law, grandparents-in-law or siblings.

speaker: The Second Minister for Manpower (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The first amendment will allow more members to make CPF transfers to their parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It describes how much CPF transfers givers can make through the CPF Retirement Sum Topping-Up Scheme.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, if Members look at the different rows, one row is for the "Amounts that can be given to the Spouse"; the second row has got to do with how much transfers can be given to the parents and grandparents; and the third row has got to do with transfers to parents-in-law, grandparents-in-law and siblings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For the purpose of our amendment Bill today, we are only looking at those transfers to parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, Members should be looking at the middle row where we described what the current practice is and what the new practice will be for both members who are aged below 55, as well members who are aged 55 and above.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Currently, when a CPF member below the age of 55 has sufficient savings in his Ordinary Account (OA) and Special Account (SA) to meet the prevailing Full Retirement Sum (FRS), he can transfer part of his OA savings to his parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For a member aged 55 and above to do likewise, the CPF Board will look at combined savings, not just in his OA and SA, but also include his Retirement Account (RA).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, we will look at all three – OA, SA and RA – and if those combined savings are sufficient to meet the FRS of his cohort, he can transfer part of his OA savings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To explain the amendment, let me first talk about the property charge.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When CPF OA savings are used to finance the property purchase, a charge is placed on the property so that if the property is subsequently sold, proceeds from the sale will be used to refund the CPF OA principal sum previously withdrawn to buy the property, plus interest the member would have earned if it had not been withdrawn.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The property charge, therefore, helps to secure the member’s CPF savings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, a member’s property charge is not currently taken into consideration when he applies to transfer part of his CPF savings to his loved ones.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: With this amendment, the property charge will be considered together with other CPF savings when assessing whether a member is eligible to make transfers to his parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For a member aged 55 and above to do likewise, CPF Board will look not just at his OA and SA but include the RA as well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If he has sufficient savings to meet his cohort BRS which, together with his property charge, is sufficient to meet his cohort FRS, he can transfer part of his OA, SA and RA savings above the BRS to his parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is why I have provided the chart for Members to refer to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But the upshot is this: whatever their ages, the members would be required to set aside the BRS in their CPF savings before they can make transfers to parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This ensures that these members have enough for their own basic retirement needs and have also added security through the property charges.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This amendment will give members more options to strengthen their parents' and grandparents' retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In particular, it will help members who want to increase their parents' or grandparents' retirement savings but may not be able to do so through cash top-ups.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second amendment updates the payout benchmark for Retirement Sum exemption.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, in addition to his CPF savings, a member may have lifelong payouts from a private annuity or pension which is higher than the monthly CPF payout that an age peer receives under the Retirement Sum Scheme (RSS).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such members have been allowed to apply to withdraw their CPF savings, without having to set aside their cohort Retirement Sum.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Those with lower private annuity or pension payouts may apply for partial exemption from setting aside their cohort Retirement Sum.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As CPF LIFE has replaced RSS as the default retirement payout scheme for members entering retirement, it is timely to update the benchmark used for Retirement Sum exemptions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead of the RSS payout, we will now use the monthly CPF LIFE payout that a member who has met the cohort FRS is expected to receive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Annually, for the past few years, about 200 members have successfully applied for full or partial exemption.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The effect of this amendment is that more members will qualify for full exemption.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The third and last set of amendments provide greater clarity and efficiency in the administration of some parts of the CPF Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, the top-up limit for transfers from the OA to the member’s own SA is prescribed in the CPF Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, all the other top-up limits, such as for CPF transfers to spouses, are prescribed in the regulations instead of the main Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The amendment will simplify the CPF Act such that all computational details for limits on voluntary top-ups to various CPF accounts will be specified in the CPF Regulations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is no change to the top-up limits, only where they are specified.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As a mandatory social security savings scheme funded by contributions from employers and employees, the CPF system is closely tied to employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This means that there will be certain groups in our populace, such as our elderly who are likely to have little to no CPF savings, who would not be able to benefit directly from the system to meet their retirement, housing and healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is in addition to the option of topping up the CPF accounts of their spouses for the same purpose at the same lowered threshold.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: While providing members with flexibility is good, I remain concerned about the trajectories of various forces which will challenge the robustness of our CPF system to meet the needs of our people's retirement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, as our life expectancy increases, the gap between our retirement age and life expectancy widens.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our statutory retirement age remains at 62 while our re-employment age has recently been raised to 67.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: According to the 2017 World Health Statistics report by the World Health Organization (WHO), the average life expectancy in Singapore is 83.1 years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The report also found that Singapore's healthy life expectancy, that is, number of years people live in full health, is 73.9 years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Assuming that one is employed up to age 67, his retirement savings must be sufficient to last him for another 16 years, of which there would likely be increased healthcare expenses for 10 years due to ill health.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is not taking into account rising healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The WHO report found that in Singapore, women could well expect to live for 86.1 years, while the average male expectancy is 80.1 years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The labour force participation rates of women, although increasing, have always been lower than their male counterparts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Based on age-gender specific resident labour force participation rates in 2016, the participation rate for females peak at 25 to 29 years at 90.6% and declines steadily thereafter to 77.2% by 45 to 49 years of age.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In comparison, the participation rate for males peak at 35 to 39 years at 97.8% and holds steady at above 90% to 50 to 54 years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: According to the Ministry of Social and Family Development's (MSF's) study on "Family and Work", women are more likely than men to remain outside the labour force for family-related responsibilities, such as housework, childcare and caregiving to families or relatives.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, the size of our families has been on the decline.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With fewer children, the older generation will have less financial support for their retirement from the younger generation and some will have none.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Our population has been ageing since 2000, with the number of residents in the older age groups increasing significantly.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: On the economic front, we are also facing uncertainties as we push on with restructuring efforts to stay ahead of the game against global headwinds of market volatility and increased protectionism.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In this climate, we are also likely to face challenges to traditional employment models.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: In view of the above trajectories, I have the following questions on the proposed amendments to the Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: First, the Ministry said that this proposed amendment will give members who are providing for their parents and grandparents more options to strengthen their parents’ and grandparents’ retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Second, I would like to request the Minister to provide examples of the types of family units which will benefit most from exercising this option to top up their parents' or grandparents' CPF accounts for their retirement needs, provide specifics on the age, salary and CPF account balances of the CPF members making the top-ups.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Third, what safeguards are in place to ensure that the member who is making top-ups of his parents’ or grandparents’ CPF accounts is adequately advised of the impact of his actions on his CPF savings for his own retirement needs?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: What are the outreach efforts to educate the public about these top-up options?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Would CPF Board be offering advisory services to members or to assist them in making informed choices on the various options available to them?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fourth, the CPF member who wishes to top up the CPF account of his parents or grandparents needs to meet the requisite BRS in his/her OA, SA as well as RA and have sufficient property pledge or charge to make up for the requisite FRS.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: For a CPF member who has met the FRS with a property pledge or charge and made top-ups to his parents' CPF account, I would like to ask the Minister what would be the impact on the member, if any, in the event that he wishes to sell his property, and what is the subject matter of the property pledge or charge and his ability to use his CPF monies to purchase a new property?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Fifth, what other alternatives are there for families of lower-wage earners with insufficient amounts in their CPF accounts and who are unable to utilise this “self-help” option to make the top-ups for their parents or grandparents for their retirement needs?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I also have some additional questions on the provision for CPF members to apply for exemption from setting aside the Retirement Sum if they have their own private annuity which provides them with payouts for life.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This option has been made available for some years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I would also like to ask the Minister what outreach efforts have been in place to educate CPF members and the financial institutions offering personal annuities which qualify for this exemption.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: As the number of options available to members increase, I urge the Minister to ensure that adequate public education and advisory services are made available to members so that they can make informed choices that would best suit their needs, especially considering the challenges that we will be facing as an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For many Singaporeans, their dreams and plans for retirement, flat ownership, or even going on a once-in-a-lifetime haj could hinge on the policy directions set by some of these amendments.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As our social security system adapts to changing times, the facts and impact of each amendment to the Act must be made known to the affected members in a simple and easy to understand manner.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This is important because, compared to the CPF of yesteryears, the scheme we have today has evolved over time to allow members options to choose the types of retirement plans or top-up schemes to support their loved ones, to name a few.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Thus, CPF members today need to make informed choices.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For this purpose, I have some brief clarifications to seek from the Minister on some of the key features of this CPF amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: First, I have some questions pertaining to the proposed amendment made to section 18 of the CPF Act.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: This amendment is to give the Board the flexibility to determine the amount of money standing to a member’s credit in CPF that can be transferred to the RA and SA of a relevant individual.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Although this feature of the 2017 CPF amendment Bill is touted as a change to strengthen family support by allowing more CPF members to make CPF transfers to their parents and grandparents, the proposed changes to section 18 of the CPF Act seem to only bring in line the changes made previously and, that is, to allow members to transfer less to their RA if they have sufficient property charge.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If they can meet the BRS, which is half of the FRS Sum, these members can withdraw their remaining CPF savings in cash when they attained the age of 55.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They can then use the cash to do a top-up of the CPF accounts of their loved ones under the Retirement Sum Topping-Up Scheme.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Members who qualify to make CPF transfer to their loved ones under the proposed amendment would most likely come from the same group who qualify to make lump-sum withdrawal from their CPF accounts in cash after setting aside their BRS and property pledge upon attaining the age of 55.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Although there is a personal income tax relief cap from Year of Assessment (YA) 2018, the incentive for cash top-up of CPF accounts remains more attractive than direct CPF transfers.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Second, I welcome the proposed amendment to section 15 to allow members who are or will be receiving a pension, annuity or other benefit approved by the Board, the flexibility to make a withdrawal from their RA subject to the payout benchmark specified by the Minister.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The differentiated “payout benchmark” is something new and, as stated in the new subsection 8CA, there are different amounts of payout benchmark for different classes of members based on the life expectancy.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I seek more information on how the Board is going to classify these annuitants based on life expectancy.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Just like the speaker before me, every amendment proposed must surely be motivated by some trending statistics, demands from account holders, or changing social norms.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Specifically, can the Minister share what CPF has found in its big data analytics to derive at the proposed changes found in this amendment Bill?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is the number of elderly Singaporeans with retirement adequacy issues rising despite having children with healthy CPF accounts?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Are there many requests from Singaporeans who want to do CPF top-ups for their loved ones?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is CPF encouraging members to borrow from their future retirement needs to pay for the current needs of their loved ones today?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is there any projection done on the retirement adequacy of these members when they grow old if they were to top up the CPF accounts of their loved ones today?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the amendments are very much about technical thresholds, payout benchmarks and administrative mechanisms, I would like to highlight the core value of filial piety that underlies these amendments.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It strengthens the idea of the family and familial relations as a key source of financial and social support by encouraging retirement planning that is based upon the ties within the family unit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we debate about the specifics and technicalities of legislation in Parliament, I believe it is important to highlight and reinforce the fundamental values we stand for as a community, like filial piety, and how this can be expressed through the legislation we pass.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I had raised a similar point when we debated the CPF (Amendment No 2) Bill and was heartened that in the reply, the Minister clarified that the CPF Retirement Sum Topping-Up Scheme included parents-in-law and grandparents-in-law.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Why then are we not extending this to this group of people now?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Tax relief is currently provided for cash top-ups, subject to conditions and caps.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Similar tax-based incentive schemes for CPF transfers may encourage those who are in a stronger financial position to top up the accounts of lower-balance or non-working family members.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have to add though that I hope they do not make transfers just for the tax reliefs.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, this scheme is premised on older CPF members having family members who are able to top up their CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am concerned about older members who do not have any immediate family members or who do not have strong ties with their family members.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share whether there are measures in place to improve retirement adequacy for this group of people who are the ones most in need of a steady income stream in their later years?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, there is a general lack of understanding of the CPF system and its policies amongst the general public.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While having greater flexibility is laudable, it also introduces more complexity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share whether they are plans to improve our communications with regard to the CPF system, especially to our seniors?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Speaker, Sir, I rise in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am in favour of the amendments to exempt CPF members who have pensions, annuities or other CPF-approved benefits which match the set benchmarks from having to top up their Retirement Sums.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These individuals have all, in their own ways, prepared and stored up equivalent financial reserves for their retirement.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Next, I also support the amendments to allow more CPF members to make transfers to their parents’ and grandparents’ RAs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will be achieved by reducing the members’ OA thresholds.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Last year, CPF had made it easier for members to transfer monies from their OA to their spouses’ SA or RA.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can CPF also expand the criteria to allow parents to transfer some of their CPF savings to their children or siblings who have special needs?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the years, a number of my residents who are not doing well financially and are unable to meet the BRS have requested to make CPF withdrawals to support the needs of such family members.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They are struggling and the assistance they receive is barely enough.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If withdrawals cannot be made, at least the transfers would afford them some peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Will the Ministry share the breakdown of these data and how many applications were successful?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to ask for the details of cash top-ups.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked for an update on the retirement adequacy of CPF members.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Retirement adequacy is improving for every successive cohort.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We expect this proportion to grow to seven in 10 for the cohort turning age 55 in 2020.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even so, there is scope to help CPF members, especially older cohorts who are already in retirement, to improve their retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why we are making it possible for more CPF members to initiate CPF transfers to their parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Which are the families that are more likely to benefit from the amendments?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Well, they first have to have a property charge and they also have to be able to meet either the prevailing or the cohort BRS which, therefore, means that they are more likely to be older in age.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked how a property sale would affect CPF members who earlier made CPF transfers to their parents after using a property pledge or charge to meet the FRS.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The property pledge or charge works to help restore CPF members’ savings to their FRS if they sell their property.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The property sale and the resulting CPF refund do not affect the earlier CPF transfers made by the member to his spouse, parents or grandparents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To be clear, those family members will retain the transferred CPF monies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Png Eng Huat had talked about the fact that if a member is aged 55 and above, he is already eligible to withdraw his CPF savings after setting aside his cohort BRS and he can use these withdrawals to give cash top-ups to his parents and grandparents and, in fact, enjoy a tax relief on it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But instead of this two-step process of a withdrawal and then a top-up, we want to be able to facilitate a transfer by allowing him to use a property charge to help meet the cohort FRS, if he wishes to transfer part of his CPF savings above the cohort BRS to his parents or grandparents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But Mr Png added that, in doing so, he does not get to enjoy the potential tax relief.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What CPF Board will do is, in interacting with the member, they can, indeed, point this out to the member that if they take a two-step approach, they are eligible for a tax relief.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It depends on whether they have income at that point in time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To some of the members, they may no longer be earning an income and, therefore, a tax relief means nothing to them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Png's question is: in making this change, will it be a white elephant?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is not the way we think about it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It can also be that a member already has an existing property charge that was made years ago.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, after he turns age 55, the property charge is there and he wants to take advantage of it, we see no reason why he should be prevented from doing so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To Mr Patrick Tay's question, making a property charge or pledge will not affect the members' ownership of the property or their right to sell in future.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, members can continue to use the sales proceeds refunded to their CPF for a future housing purchase in accordance with the prevailing CPF rules.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about flexibility for members to transfer CPF savings to their spouses.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As discussed in this House last year, we reduced the threshold from FRS to BRS so that more members can make CPF transfers to their spouses' accounts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, if my memory serves me right, about 75% of all CPF transfers made last year were made to spouses rather than to someone else.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is already a lower threshold than for CPF transfers to parents and grandparents and will remain so even after this round of amendments.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether the amendment will also apply to parents-in-law and grandparents-in-law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, members can already transfer CPF savings above the FRS to their parents-in-law and grandparents-in-law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I fully agree with Mr Louis Ng that we should continue to encourage filial piety, including their parents-in-law and grandparents-in-law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, we also need to strike a balance between protecting the member’s retirement adequacy and enabling him to support his older family members’ retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why we are making a concession to lower the threshold only for CPF transfers to parents and grandparents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Nevertheless, members who want to use the concessionary threshold for CPF transfers to their parents-in-law and grandparents-in-law can approach CPF Board and these requests will be considered on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh further asked about flexibilities for CPF transfers to children or siblings with special needs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Currently, CPF members can use their MediSave savings to pay for their children or siblings’ healthcare.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They can also use their OA savings to provide a loan for their children’s tertiary education.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition, parents can make use of the Special Needs Savings Scheme to set aside CPF savings for the long-term care of their children with special needs.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under this scheme, the parents’ CPF savings can be used to provide the children with a stream of monthly payouts upon the parents’ demise.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Patrick Tay asked whether the transferred CPF monies could be returned to the giver's CPF accounts upon the demise of the recipient.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, it depends on whether they have been streamed out and, if they have been streamed out, there is nothing to refund.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But if they have not been streamed out, yes, then there is something to be refunded.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng asked whether tax relief could be given for CPF transfers between members.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Hence, CPF monies transferred from one member’s account to another have already enjoyed tax relief.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But this does not mean that there is no additional benefit to making such CPF transfers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, CPF transfers often allow families to maximise the interest earned on their combined CPF savings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, there is benefit in terms of the interest that can be earned even though there is no additional tax relief.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: CPF Board has stepped up its member engagement efforts.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Throughout this year, CPF Board has organised retirement planning roadshows, talks and mobile service centres across Singapore to reach out directly to members.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And just this past weekend, CPF Board ran a roadshow in Sengkang.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We also recognise that even with all of these engagements and outreach, sometimes we remember best when we need to do something with the information.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, CPF Board provides a retirement planning service.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, this is face-to-face, one-on-one, and the members have the chance to ask for clarification until it is clear to them what they are getting themselves into.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There may be others that do not pertain directly to the specifics of this Bill and I ask for the Members' understanding.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I think a better time to address them would have to be found.
